question: The world's oldest continuously operating university was founded in the year 859 by a woman named Fatima al-Fihri. In which country is it?

extra.why_interesting: The oldest university still running was founded by a woman in Africa, not in Europe.
extra.verification_notes: al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco is confirmed by Guinness World Records and UNESCO as founded 859 by Fatima al-Fihri; the scholarly Bologna dispute contests the 'oldest university' framing but yields no alternative country answer (https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/oldest-university).

explanation: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, is recognised by UNESCO and Guinness as the oldest continuously operating degree-granting university, predating Bologna by over two centuries.

question: In the 1850s, Emperor Napoleon III reportedly served his most honoured guests with cutlery made of a rare metal, while lesser guests had to settle for gold. What metal was it?

extra.why_interesting: The metal we now wrap sandwiches in was once literally more precious than gold. Framing it as a dinner-table status symbol makes the reversal vivid.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's History of aluminium states the anecdote in matching terms — 'Napoleon is reputed to have held a banquet where the most honored guests were given aluminium utensils while others made do with gold' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_aluminium) — and the question's 'reportedly' correctly signals the story's unverified status; no rival metal or newer development found.

explanation: Before the Hall-Héroult electrolysis process was developed in 1886, extracting aluminium from ore was so difficult that it cost more than gold. The peak of the Washington Monument was capped with it as a luxury material in 1884, just before the price collapsed.

question: What happened first: the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza, or the death of the last woolly mammoths?

extra.why_interesting: People picture mammoths as Ice Age creatures and pyramids as 'history', so learning they overlapped is a genuine shock.
extra.verification_notes: The Great Pyramid dates to c. 2600 BC (~4,600 BP) while the last woolly mammoths on Wrangel Island survived until ~4,000 BP (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolly_mammoth), a gap reaffirmed by the 2024 Cell genome study.

explanation: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC. A dwarf population of woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 2000 BC, so the pyramid stood for roughly five centuries while mammoths still walked the Earth.

question: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest man-made structure on Earth for how long?
review_notes: founder rating 9/10 (2026-09-03): to uz mohla byt mcq otazka, ale ok, zabavna

extra.why_interesting: The correct option is the most extreme one, and the player can reason about when tall cathedrals appeared in Europe.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives 'more than 3,700 years' (surpassed mid-13th c. by Old St Paul's) and elsewhere Lincoln Cathedral in 1311 (~3,870 years); both land far closer to 3,800 than to the other options — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza

explanation: Completed around 2560 BC at about 146 metres, the pyramid was only overtaken around AD 1311 by the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England. That is a record of nearly 3,800 years that no building is likely to match.

question: In 1908, a German housewife named Melitta Bentz tore a sheet of blotting paper out of her son's school exercise book, punched holes in a brass pot, and invented what kitchen item that still carries her name?

extra.why_interesting: A kitchen staple was invented by a frustrated housewife using paper from her child's schoolbook, and her surname is still printed on the product in shops today.
extra.verification_notes: DPMA (German Patent and Trade Mark Office) confirms Dresden housewife Melitta Bentz used blotting paper from her son's exercise book in a perforated brass cup in 1908 to create the coffee filter, and the Melitta brand remains active (€2.53bn revenue in 2025): https://www.dpma.de/english/our_office/publications/ingeniouswomen/110jahrekaffeefilter/index.html

explanation: Fed up with bitter coffee full of grounds, Melitta Bentz used the absorbent blotting paper to strain her brew. She patented the paper coffee filter the same year, and the Melitta company she founded in Dresden still sells filters around the world.

question: Long before it ever touched a tree, the chainsaw was invented in the 1780s by two Scottish doctors to speed up what medical procedure?
review_notes: founder rating 9/10 (2026-09-03): velmi zaujimave ak to je fakt pravda

extra.why_interesting: A tool now used for felling trees began life in an operating room, and the actual procedure is startling. Players reason backward from 'what would doctors need to cut?'
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chainsaw) and Snopes confirm Aitken and Jeffray devised the chain saw c. 1783-85 for symphysiotomy in obstructed labour; the only quibble is that Jeffray's own aim was excision of diseased bone rather than childbirth, which does not change the intended answer.

explanation: The first chainsaw was a small hand-cranked chain of teeth used to cut through the pelvic bone when a baby was stuck during delivery, a procedure called symphysiotomy. It replaced a knife and saw, and only much later was the idea scaled up for cutting wood.

question: Champagne is one of the coldest wine regions in France, and its winemakers originally considered the bubbles a defect. How did the cold climate accidentally create those bubbles in the first place?
correct_answer: Cold paused fermentation, spring restarted it in bottle
alternative_answers: Fermentation stopped in winter and restarted in spring inside sealed bottles
Yeast went dormant in the cold and reawakened in warm weather after bottling
Wine was bottled before fermentation finished, so it fermented again in the bottle
Second fermentation in the bottle trapped carbon dioxide
Unfinished fermentation resumed after bottling and trapped the gas
headline_answer: Cold paused fermentation, spring restarted it in bottle
review_notes: founder rating 9/10 (2026-09-03): uff tak to je dost komplikovana odpoved. neviem si predstavit ako ju llm vyhodnoti, ale inak velmi zaujimave. mozno mcq by bolo lepsie?

extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's History of Champagne and Sparkling wine articles and the Union des Maisons de Champagne all confirm that cold cellars halted fermentation, leaving sugar and dormant yeast that refermented in bottle come spring (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Champagne), and Wikipedia explicitly notes the resulting fizz 'was considered a wine fault' in early Champagne winemaking.

explanation: Autumn in Champagne turned cold so quickly that the yeast went dormant before it had eaten all the sugar in the grape juice. Winemakers assumed fermentation was finished and bottled the wine. When spring warmed the cellars, the yeast woke up and resumed fermenting inside the sealed bottles. The carbon dioxide had nowhere to escape, so it dissolved into the wine as bubbles, and the pressure often burst the bottles. For a long time this was seen as a flaw, until sparkling wine became fashionable and the process was deliberately controlled.

question: A goatherd in Ethiopia noticed his goats leaping about with energy after chewing red berries from a bush. What drink does this legend claim to explain?
review_notes: founder rating 8/10 (2026-09-03): zvlastne poskladana otazka, tazko sa chape. inak zaujimave.

extra.why_interesting: A drink half the world starts its day with is explained by a folk tale about hyperactive goats, and the player can deduce it from the 'energy' clue.
extra.verification_notes: The legend of the Ethiopian goatherd (later named Kaldi) whose goats grew lively after eating red berries is the standard origin myth for coffee, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaldi and the National Coffee Association; the question correctly frames it as a legend's claim.

explanation: The legend of Kaldi the goatherd is the traditional origin story of coffee. Ethiopia is the plant's native home, and the goats' 'dancing' supposedly led monks to brew the berries to stay awake during prayers.

question: How many bones are inside an elephant's trunk?

extra.why_interesting: Players know the trunk is flexible, but the answer of zero bones plus tens of thousands of muscles is still startling.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's elephant article and the biomechanics literature both state the trunk is a boneless muscular hydrostat (up to 150,000 muscle fascicles, no bone), so zero is correct and the fact is not time-sensitive: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elephant

explanation: The trunk contains no bones at all. It is made of roughly 40,000 muscle units, which is why it can lift a log and also pick up a single peanut.

question: One colourful crustacean strikes so fast that its punch creates bubbles of boiling water and has been known to crack aquarium glass. Name it.

extra.why_interesting: A hand-sized crustacean punching hard enough to boil water and break glass is a genuine wonder of nature.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the smasher mantis shrimp's ~23 m/s strike generates vapour-filled cavitation bubbles and that accounts of it breaking glass tanks exist (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantis_shrimp); the colour/punch/glass cues exclude the pistol shrimp alternative and nothing recent supersedes it.

explanation: The mantis shrimp's club accelerates like a bullet, reaching around 80 km/h in a few thousandths of a second. The strike is so fast it creates cavitation bubbles that collapse with a flash of heat and light.

question: A sperm whale hunts squid more than a kilometre below the surface. How long can it hold its breath on a single dive?
review_notes: founder rating 10/10 (2026-09-03): znova mohla byt mcq

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows whales must surface to breathe, but almost nobody has a feel for how long a sperm whale can actually stay down. Ninety minutes sits far beyond any human reference point, yet the player can reason their way there: whales are air-breathing mammals, so hours seems impossible, but sperm whales hunt giant squid a kilometre down, so a few minutes is clearly too short.
extra.verification_notes: Sperm whales typically dive 35-45 minutes and can hold their breath up to ~90-120 minutes (a 117-minute dive is documented), so of the three options 90 minutes is uniquely correct; depth premise and answer are both supported by https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperm_whale

explanation: Sperm whales routinely dive for 45 minutes and can stay under for around 90 minutes on a deep hunt. They manage this by storing oxygen in their muscles and blood rather than their lungs, slowing their heart rate, and letting their ribcage collapse under pressure. Six hours is beyond any mammal, while 15 minutes would not even get them to their hunting depth and back.

question: Which is hotter: the surface of the Sun or a bolt of lightning?

extra.why_interesting: Most people assume nothing on Earth beats the Sun for heat, but a lightning channel is roughly five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
extra.verification_notes: Lightning's return-stroke channel exceeds 27,800 °C (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning) versus the Sun's photosphere at ~5,772 K (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosphere), so lightning is ~5x hotter; 'surface' correctly excludes the million-degree corona.

explanation: A lightning channel briefly reaches around 30,000 degrees Celsius, while the Sun's visible surface is only about 5,500 degrees. The Sun's core is far hotter, but its surface loses to a summer thunderstorm.

question: True or false: if the air gets cold enough, it becomes physically impossible for snow to fall.

extra.why_interesting: The phrase 'too cold to snow' is repeated every winter, yet it is a myth. Snow can fall at any temperature below freezing if there is moisture.
extra.verification_notes: NSIDC states 'While it can be too warm to snow, it cannot be too cold to snow' and NWS says 'It's never too cold for snow, but perhaps too dry' (https://nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/snow/science-snow), confirming the claimed answer of False.

explanation: False. Snow can fall at any temperature below freezing, and it has been recorded at minus 40 degrees and colder. Very cold air holds much less moisture, so heavy snowfalls become rare, but there is no temperature at which snow becomes impossible.

question: How fast does a large raindrop hit the ground?

extra.why_interesting: Raindrops feel fast when they hit your face, but air resistance caps them at roughly the speed of a sprinter.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Rain article gives large 5 mm drops an impact speed of ~9 m/s (20 mph), which matches sprinting speed rather than walking (~3 mph) or highway driving (~65 mph): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain

explanation: Air resistance limits large raindrops to a terminal velocity of about 9 metres per second, roughly 32 kilometres per hour. That is about the speed of a good sprinter. Drizzle falls far more slowly, and no raindrop ever reaches highway speed.

question: Name the Pacific climate pattern that Peruvian fishermen named after the baby Jesus, because its warm waters tended to arrive around Christmas.

extra.why_interesting: A world-changing climate pattern got its name from a Christmas timing quirk noticed by fishermen.
extra.verification_notes: NOAA Climate.gov and PMEL confirm Peruvian fishermen named the warm coastal current 'El Niño' after the Christ Child for its Christmastime arrival; the etymology is historical and cannot be made stale (https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/what-el-ni%C3%B1o%E2%80%93southern-oscillation-enso-nutshell).

explanation: El Niño is Spanish for 'the boy' and refers to the Christ child. Fishermen off Peru noticed the unusually warm current appearing in late December. The pattern warms the eastern Pacific every few years and shifts rainfall, droughts and storms across the globe. Its cool opposite is called La Niña.

question: Count the seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder, then divide by three. What does the result tell you?
correct_answer: Distance to the lightning in kilometres
alternative_answers: how far away the lightning is
how many kilometres away the storm is

extra.why_interesting: A folk trick everyone has heard turns out to be real physics: sound takes about three seconds per kilometre.
extra.verification_notes: Sound travels ~1 km per 3 seconds, so dividing the flash-to-bang delay by three gives the distance to the strike in kilometres, as stated in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder; the fact is a physical constant and cannot be superseded.

explanation: Light reaches you almost instantly, but sound travels at about 340 metres per second, so it needs roughly three seconds to cover one kilometre. Dividing the delay by three gives the distance to the strike in kilometres. Dividing by five gives it in miles.

question: Invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who hoped it would bring peace between quarrelling nations, what is the world's most widely spoken constructed language?

extra.why_interesting: An eye doctor building an entire language to end ethnic strife is an unexpectedly idealistic origin story
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Zamenhof, a Polish-Jewish ophthalmologist, published Esperanto in 1887 to promote peace, and calls it 'the world's most widely spoken constructed auxiliary language' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanto); no rival conlang has overtaken it.

explanation: Ludwik Zamenhof grew up in multilingual Białystok, where Poles, Russians, Germans and Jews often clashed. He designed Esperanto as a simple neutral second language for everyone, and it still has an active worldwide community today.

question: Papua New Guinea has more living languages than any other country on Earth. How many?

extra.why_interesting: A single medium-sized country holding more than a tenth of all human languages challenges every assumption about linguistic diversity
extra.verification_notes: Ethnologue lists 840 living languages for Papua New Guinea (839-841 across editions), the most of any country and clearly closest to 800; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_number_of_languages

explanation: Roughly 840 distinct languages are spoken in Papua New Guinea, more than a tenth of all languages in the world. Rugged mountains and isolated valleys kept communities apart for thousands of years, so each developed its own tongue.
